title: A Better Kind of Jealousy
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The rumor reached Greg before I got back from Brasswatch.

I found him sitting on the hood of the van with a paper cup of coffee and the look he wore when he was trying to decide whether a joke would make something less painful.

"Hey," he said.

"Hey."

He smiled too quickly.

"Busy day?"

"Very. Danse finally got the workshop door working without a lock you need a ladder to reach."

"That's good."

"Greg."

"What?"

"What's wrong?"

He stared into his coffee.

"Nothing. Just heard a weird thing."

I waited.

He sighed.

"Somebody said you're planning to move into Brasswatch permanently. That you and Danse are making some kind of big announcement. That I'm basically the guy you visit when there's music."

I blinked.

"Who said that?"

"Does it matter?"

"It matters that someone is inventing a story about my life."

Greg tried to laugh.

"Yeah, well, people like a good story."

"That doesn't make it true."

He shrugged, still looking at the cup.

I sat beside him, close enough that our shoulders touched but not so close that he couldn't move away.

"Do you believe it?" I asked.

"No." He hesitated. "Not exactly."

"Then what is it?"

He rubbed the heel of his hand against his forehead.

"I know what we agreed. I know you're ethically non-monogamous, that you prefer polyamory, and that none of this means you're promising to be exclusive with me. I've said yes to being part of your life because I want to be here."

"I know."

"But sometimes I hear people talk like there's a scoreboard, and I start wondering if I'm losing."

The words were plain enough to make my chest tighten.

"Greg."

He looked at me.

"I'm not proud of that."

"You don't have to be ashamed of feeling insecure."

"I don't want to turn into somebody who needs to know where you are every minute."

"Then don't. Tell me what you're afraid of."

He took a long breath.

"That one day you'll find somebody whose life fits yours better. Somebody who can build things, fight monsters, fix doors, whatever. And I'll be the guy who makes you laugh until you don't need that anymore."

I looked at his hands, rough from strings and work. I thought about the fundraiser, the way he'd learned to say no to a song that hurt him, and the small note he'd left on the dashboard reminding himself not to promise the universe on my behalf.

"You're not a consolation prize," I said.

He smiled faintly.

"Wasn't planning to enter a competition."

"Good. Because there isn't one."

He took another breath.

"I know jealousy doesn't mean somebody's done something wrong."

"Sometimes it tells us we need something. Time. Reassurance. A clearer plan."

He looked at me.

"Can I ask for a clearer plan?"

"Please."

We went inside the little house near the beach and sat at the kitchen table. Greg set the coffee aside and took out a pencil. I brought my notebook.

We talked about what was actually changing.

I was helping Danse with the workshop and spending more time at Brasswatch during repairs. That didn't mean I was moving there. Iroh's teahouse needed help after the roof leak. Riverstone's bridge working group had a schedule I wanted to respect. I still wanted time with Greg in Beach City and at Starwake Pier.

"You could have told me the Brasswatch work was taking more hours," he said.

"I thought I had."

"You told me about the door. Not about the whole week."

I winced.

"You're right."

He nodded.

"I'm not asking you to report to me. I just want to know when our plans are likely to change."

"That's fair."

We checked the calendar.

Greg wanted a regular evening to play music together, even if I was terrible at it. I wanted one day a month where we could go somewhere without turning the outing into a community service project. He needed the freedom to visit Steven without assuming I'd always come along. I needed him to be able to tell me when gossip hurt instead of pretending it was funny.

"That last one sounds hard," he said.

"It is."

"I can try."

"That's all I'm asking."

He wrote something in the margin.

I leaned over.

"What's that?"

"Official Greg Rule Number One."

I read it.

DON'T LET STRANGERS WRITE YOUR LOVE SONGS.

I laughed.

"That's a good rule."

"Number Two is probably don't drink three cups of coffee before discussing feelings."

"Also good."

He glanced at me.

"Can I ask one more thing?"

"Of course."

"If you ever do make a big change, will you tell me yourself?"

"Yes. Not because you own the decision. Because you matter to me."

He looked relieved.

"Okay."

We sat for a while without talking. The house smelled of coffee and salt air. A gull called outside, then another answered. Somewhere down the street, a car door slammed.

Greg reached for my hand.

"I love you," he said.

"I love you too."

He smiled, slow and genuine.

Then he leaned forward, stopped just short of my face, and raised an eyebrow.

"Am I allowed to kiss you, or do I need to schedule it?"

"You can kiss me."

"Good. I was running out of paperwork."

His kiss was warm and a little clumsy. I laughed against his mouth. He pulled back, grinning.

"There. Much better than coffee."

"Depends on the coffee."

"Rude."

I kissed him again.

The rest of the afternoon belonged to an ordinary day together. We washed the dishes, fixed a loose hinge on a cupboard, and took a walk along the boardwalk. Greg stopped to talk to a musician he knew, and I bought a small packet of sea-salt candy from a shop near the pier.

We didn't solve jealousy forever.

At dinner, Greg admitted he still felt a little nervous about the rumor.

I told him he could ask me again if he needed reassurance, and I would answer honestly rather than make him feel foolish.

He nodded.

"Then I'm going to ask something very important."

"What?"

"Are you staying for the movie?"

I smiled.

"Yes."

"Great. Because I've already made popcorn."

Later, when the lights were low and the movie had become background noise, he rested his head against my shoulder. I brushed my fingers through his hair, and he took my hand without looking away from the screen.

Outside, the tide moved in and out along Beach City.

It had always done that.

It didn't have to choose one shore forever to keep returning.
